performers: Hochschulsymphonieorchester, University of Music and Theatre Munich; Marcus Bosch, conductor
question: How does a finale answer the first movement without repeating it?
intro: The finale begins on violin tremolo, as the symphony did, and its first theme is a close relative of the opening melody, sharpened into a double-dotted rhythm. Follow three theme groups, a recapitulation that reverses their order, and a coda where the timpani return after a long silence. The file ends with about fifty seconds of what sounds like applause. All four movements of this set come from one live concert.

sections.label: First group · tremolo, then the sharpened theme
Second group · chorale in A♭ major
Third group · octave theme, A minor
Chorale returns · Tempo I
sections.mNote: chorale returns, matched at a different pitch level

cues.title: Tremolo, as at the start
cues.text: The finale opens on violin tremolo, just as the first movement did, almost inaudibly at first. Listen for the way the sound rises from near silence before any melody settles.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia (“Like the first movement, the fourth movement opens with tremolo strings”) and the first page of the score (printed p. 71, strings only) agree. The level is −48.7 dB at 0:00 and −41.3 dB at 0:05, rising to −30.7 dB at 0:10.

cues.title: The opening theme, sharpened
cues.text: The first theme enters at about 0:20, a close relative of the first movement’s opening melody, now bouncing on a double-dotted rhythm. The Hungarian Philharmonic note says the long and short notes stand in the ratio 7:1 instead of 3:1.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −42.4 dB at 0:15 to −28.4 dB at 0:20 and −17.2 dB at 0:25. The relation to the first movement and the 7:1 ratio are from the Hungarian Philharmonic note; the score marks letter A at the start of the second system on printed p. 71.

cues.title: Two faces of one theme
cues.text: The Berlin Philharmonic’s note says this jaunty theme is more or less the symphony’s opening notes, differently orchestrated, rhythmised, shortened and accelerated. Few listeners notice on first hearing. Bruckner reveals the link only in the final nine bars.
cues.evidence: The Berlin Philharmonic programme note makes the claim and names the last nine bars; the LA Phil note likewise says the finale’s first theme shares the basic outline of the first movement’s.

cues.title: A chorale in A♭ major
cues.text: At about a minute the music turns quiet and slower, in the distant key of A♭ major. This second group is a religious chorale with chromatic, Tristan-like harmony, according to the Hungarian Philharmonic note.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 0:58 (0.50); the level falls from −19.4 dB at 0:50 to −33.7 dB at 1:00 with 0.0–0.2 onsets per second, and the local key is A♭ major (0.73) at 0:55. The key is from Wikipedia and the character from the Hungarian Philharmonic note; the score puts a slower metronome mark at letter C (printed p. 72) and shows Wagner-tuba parts by letter D (printed p. 73).

cues.title: Keys a major third apart
cues.text: A Munich analysis of this recording notes that Bruckner’s keys in the finale relate mostly by major thirds, which divide the tonal space into three equal parts, rather than by the usual fifths. Listen for harmony that steps sideways instead of resolving.
cues.evidence: The Munich analysis page states the major-third plan for the finale; this is a listening suggestion for the whole chorale stretch, not a timed modulation. The level stays between −19.6 and −34.2 dB from 1:30 to 2:35 with at most 1.2 onsets per second.

cues.title: Finished on holiday
cues.text: Bruckner completed the finale during his summer holiday of 1883. The sketch is dated 10 August and the score 5 September. The finale was done about two years after the date on the first page of the first movement, 23 September 1881.
cues.evidence: Cohrs’s Hyperion booklet note gives the sketch and score dates and the date on the first page of the autograph of the first movement: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: No Wagner tubas at first
cues.text: A surviving discarded first page of the finale has no staves for Wagner tubas, so Bruckner apparently first planned the movement without them, according to Cohrs, who edited the score. The tubas appear in the finished movement.
cues.evidence: Cohrs’s Hyperion booklet note describes the discarded bifolio with no tuba staves; the first edition shows tuba staves with notes at letter D (printed p. 73).

cues.title: The octave theme in A minor
cues.text: At about 2:50 the whole orchestra plays the third group, a theme built on octaves, in A minor. After the quiet chorale this is a sudden change: the level rises about 10 dB in five seconds and notes arrive two or three times a second.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −25.8 dB at 2:45 to −15.3 dB at 2:50; onsets rise from 0.0 to 1.8–2.8 per second at 2:50–3:00; the report has a boundary at 2:54 (0.50); the local key is A minor (0.58–0.72) at 2:40–2:55. Wikipedia names the octave theme, the key and the whole orchestra.

cues.title: A long, heavy tutti
cues.text: From about 3:00 to 3:30 the level holds near −11 dB, among the loudest stretches of the movement. The score marks the section “schwer” — heavy — and asks the strings to bow “immer markig” — always strongly.
cues.evidence: The level is −11.7 dB at 3:00, −10.4 dB at 3:10 and −10.9 dB at 3:20, then −15.8 dB at 3:30. The score marks letter F “schwer” and the strings “immer markig gestrichen” with a full tutti on printed pp. 75–77.

cues.title: A finale like Haydn’s?
cues.text: The conductor Georg Tintner compared this finale to the finale of a Haydn symphony. It is much shorter than the finales of Bruckner’s Fifth and Eighth, which sum up their symphonies. The comparison is Tintner’s opinion.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s article on the symphony reports Tintner’s comparison and contrasts this finale with those of the Fifth and Eighth; the Hungarian Philharmonic note gives the lengths (about 13 minutes against 22 for the first movement, approximate).

cues.title: A hush on C
cues.text: At about 4:04 the tutti has given way to near silence. The bass sits on C, notes almost stop, and the score is marked “ruhig” — calm. The sound resumes at about 4:40 with an “a tempo” in A♭ major.
cues.evidence: The level falls from −24.1 dB at 3:55 to −33.7 dB at 4:00; the report has boundaries at 4:04 (0.71) and 4:42 (0.77), with the bass on C and 0.0–0.8 onsets per second at 4:05–4:35. The score marks letter L “Ruhig” and letter M “a tempo” (printed p. 79); the local-key estimates at 4:40–4:50 are A♭ major (0.69–0.76).

cues.title: Wolf and Levi: “incomprehensible”
cues.text: Both the composer Hugo Wolf and the conductor Hermann Levi found parts of this finale incomprehensible, the Hungarian Philharmonic’s note says. Both later came round to its unique beauty. Levi went on to call the whole symphony a Wunderwerk.
cues.evidence: The Hungarian Philharmonic note gives both men’s reaction and Levi’s Wunderwerk; the level stays between −32.5 and −43.5 dB across 4:15–4:35.

cues.title: The strongest break in the file
cues.text: At about 5:04 comes the largest structural break in the file. The level falls from −24 dB to −32 dB and the pitch centre moves to E. The score marks a new letter, N, here.
cues.evidence: The report’s strongest boundary is at 5:04 (novelty 1.00): the level falls from −23.6 dB at 5:00 to −31.7 dB at 5:05, and the local-key estimate is E major (0.57–0.73) at 5:05–5:25. The score marks letter N on printed p. 80; the estimate is approximate.

cues.title: In strict time, with a mirror
cues.text: At about 5:28 letter O is marked “Streng im Zeitmaß” — in strict time. A little earlier, around bar 163, a Munich analysis finds the movement’s main motive set in mirror image.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 5:28 (0.74), with the level at −32.6 dB at 5:25 and 1.2–2.0 onsets per second at 5:30–5:35. The score marks letter O “Streng im Zeitmaß” (printed p. 80); bar 163 is from the Munich analysis, and its time is proportioned from the pencilled bar numbers on the scan and the report’s boundaries, so approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The heavy tutti returns
cues.text: From about 6:05 the full orchestra swells back to the loudness of the 3:00 tutti, with winds and brass marked “marc.” Later the score reads “Breit und wuchtig” — broad and weighty — and the level holds near −10 dB.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −41.1 dB at 6:00 to −27.5 dB at 6:05, −13.8 dB at 6:20 and −9.9 dB at 6:30, and stays between −9.7 and −11.2 dB at 6:40–6:55; onsets are 2.0–3.0 per second at 6:40–6:50. The score marks letter P “marc. sempre” and letter Q “Breit und wuchtig” (printed pp. 81 and 83).

cues.title: Broad and weighty, almost without rest
cues.text: From about 6:40 to 7:05 the level stays between −8 and −14 dB. Listen for how the pulse hardly pauses before the block ends. At letter R the score adds “immer breiter” — ever broader.
cues.evidence: The level is −11.2 dB at 6:40, −10.4 dB at 6:45, −9.7 dB at 6:50, −9.2 dB at 6:55, −14.1 dB at 7:00 and −7.8 dB at 7:05. The score marks letter R “immer breiter” on printed p. 84.

cues.title: The block cuts off; the chorale returns
cues.text: At about 7:05–7:10 the tutti stops dead: the level falls by about 35 dB within five seconds, and the quiet chorale returns at “Tempo I”. The Hungarian Philharmonic note says the groups come back in reverse order in this recapitulation.
cues.evidence: The level falls from −7.8 dB at 7:05 to −42.9 dB at 7:10 (boundary 0.65 at 7:08) and is −28.9 dB at 7:15; a transposition-invariant chroma match between the opening of the chorale (0:58–1:38) and 7:12 scores 0.65, against 0.45 or less at every other window tested. The score marks letter S “Tempo I” (printed p. 85).

cues.title: Nikisch plays it through
cues.text: Arthur Nikisch played the new symphony through on two pianos with Bruckner’s student Josef Schalk, and at once decided to conduct it with the Gewandhaus Orchestra in Leipzig. That led to the premiere on 30 December 1884.
cues.evidence: The Hungarian Philharmonic note gives the two-piano play-through with Josef Schalk and Nikisch’s decision; the Berlin Philharmonic note and IMSLP give the premiere date and the Gewandhaus Orchestra.

cues.title: “The most important since 1827”
cues.text: Bruckner reported to a friend in Linz that Hermann Levi had called the Seventh the most important symphonic work since 1827, the year Beethoven died. Levi conducted the Munich performance on 10 March 1885, which was a great success.
cues.evidence: The Hungarian Philharmonic note quotes Levi’s remark as reported by Bruckner; Cohrs’s Hyperion note gives the Munich performance date and Levi as conductor.

cues.title: A broad tutti begins
cues.text: At about 8:20 the score marks letter V “Breit” — broad — and the whole orchestra drops into a weighty fortissimo, with “marc.” in the winds and brass. The level jumps about 12 dB in five seconds and holds near −10 dB until about 9:05.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 8:20 (0.47); the level rises from −26.6 dB at 8:20 to −14.7 dB at 8:25 and −9.2 dB at 8:40, and stays between −8.7 and −11.5 dB until 9:05. The score marks letter V “Breit” (printed p. 88).

cues.title: The theme against its mirror
cues.text: Around bar 275 a Munich analysis finds the movement’s main motive worked as a mirror canon: the theme sounds against its own inversion. It falls inside this loud block, at about 8:50, and is one example of the contrapuntal craft that runs through the finale.
cues.evidence: Bar 275 is from the Munich analysis page, which also gives bar 163 for the mirror form. The time is proportioned from the pencilled bar numbers on the scan and the report’s boundaries (the loud block 8:20–9:05), so approximate; the score marks letter W “Tempo I” on printed p. 91.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The block stops, again
cues.text: At about 9:08 the tutti is cut short: the level falls by about 12 dB in five seconds and by about 21 dB in ten. The music does not resolve; it drops into a much quieter passage.
cues.evidence: The level is −10.4 dB at 9:05, −22.3 dB at 9:10 and −31.7 dB at 9:15. The score marks a “ritard.” and diminuendo before letter X (printed pp. 92–93).

cues.title: Gathering for the coda
cues.text: From about 9:20 a quiet figure at “a tempo” grows by stages: letter X is pianissimo, and at letter Y the score asks for a crescendo. Listen for the sound swelling and falling back more than once before the end.
cues.evidence: The level moves between −31.7 dB and −17.3 dB at 9:15–9:35, with a dip to −39.6 dB at 9:45 and a rise to −11.3 dB at 10:10. The score marks letter X “a tempo” and letter Y “poco a poco cresc.” (printed pp. 93–94).

cues.title: A last broad peak
cues.text: At about 10:10 the level leaps to a broad peak near −9 dB that lasts about fifteen seconds. The score marks “Sehr breit” — very broad — just before letter Z, and then the sound stops short.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −24.1 dB at 10:05 to −11.3 dB at 10:10 and −8.4 dB at 10:20, then falls to −31.4 dB at 10:30; the report has boundaries at 10:26 (0.64) and 10:30 (0.59). The score marks “Sehr breit” at the top of printed p. 96, before letter Z.

cues.title: The timpani return
cues.text: At about 10:28 the coda begins “anfangs noch sehr ruhig” — at first still very calm — with the timpani returning after a long silence. The Hungarian Philharmonic note says they enter with an extended tremolo, as at the end of the first movement.
cues.evidence: The level falls from −11.6 dB at 10:25 to −31.4 dB at 10:30 and −26.2 dB at 10:35; the report has boundaries at 10:26 and 10:30; the audio cannot identify the timpani. The score marks letter Z “Tempo I (anfangs noch sehr ruhig)” with the timpani staff active (printed p. 96); the Hungarian Philharmonic note describes the tremolo and the earlier silence of the timpani.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The final crescendo
cues.text: From 10:40 the sound climbs steadily, about 14 dB in twenty seconds, over a timpani tremolo, to a level that stays within about two decibels until the end. Wikipedia says the timpani rolls swell before the orchestra’s tutti in the last bars.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −18.8 dB at 10:40 to −12.3 dB at 10:45, −7.2 dB at 10:55 and −4.9 dB at 11:00, then stays between −5.6 and −7.0 dB until 11:20. The coda’s timpani are from the Hungarian Philharmonic note and Wikipedia.

cues.title: The opening theme comes home
cues.text: In the last nine bars, the Berlin Philharmonic’s note says, Bruckner turns the rousing descendant back into the solemn original form of the symphony’s opening. The Munich analysis says the movement ends on a broad E major sonority in which the horns celebrate the triad.
cues.evidence: The Berlin Philharmonic note gives the last nine bars and the transformation; the Munich analysis page describes the E major sonority and the horns; the level is between −5.6 and −7.0 dB at 11:00–11:20. The time of the last nine bars is approximate.

cues.title: The music ends; applause follows
cues.text: The final chord stops between 11:20 and 11:25, and the level falls to −49 dB. After a few seconds the file continues with nearly a minute of steady, bright, unpitched sound at around −15 dB. It is consistent with audience applause, and it is not music.
cues.evidence: The level is −5.6 dB at 11:20, −48.7 dB at 11:25 and −32.5 dB at 11:30, then −14.8 to −17.6 dB for 11:35–12:10 with the centroid near 2,480 Hz and 0.2–1.0 onsets per second. That this is applause is an inference from the sound alone; the file is 754 s long.

transitions.title: The loud opening fades into a chorale
transitions.how: The first group ends in a crest near −17 dB, then thins out. At about 0:58 the music turns quieter and slower and settles in the distant key of A♭ major. The dotted, bouncing first theme gives way to a chorale with chromatic, Tristan-like harmony. At letter C the first edition prints a slower metronome mark, so the second group sounds like another kind of music rather than a continuation of the first.
transitions.evidence: The level is −19.4 dB at 0:50, −27.1 dB at 0:55 and −33.7 dB at 1:00 with onsets 0.0–0.2 per second; the report has a boundary at 0:58 (0.50). The key is from Wikipedia and the Hungarian Philharmonic note describes the chorale; the score marks a slower tempo at letter C (printed p. 72).

transitions.title: From the chorale to a heavy tutti
transitions.how: The chorale sinks into long quiet, then at about 2:50 the whole orchestra plays the octave theme in A minor. Bruckner moves from the A♭-major region of the chorale to A minor, a semitone higher, without a transitional bridge. The level rises about 10 dB in five seconds, and the section is marked “schwer” — heavy — with strongly bowed strings, which gives the music a new, rhythmic character.
transitions.evidence: The level rises from −25.8 dB at 2:45 to −15.3 dB at 2:50 and onsets from 0.0 to 1.8–2.8 per second; the report has a boundary at 2:54 (0.50) and the local key is A minor (0.58–0.72) at 2:40–2:55. The keys of the second and third groups are from Wikipedia; the score marks letter F “schwer” (printed p. 75).

transitions.title: The tutti dissolves into calm on C
transitions.how: The heavy tutti loses force over about thirty seconds, from −15 dB at 3:30 to −33.7 dB at 4:00, and the music settles into the passage marked “ruhig” at letter L. The strings drop out; the bass holds C, and the score shows a timpani C. After a pause the music resumes at letter M, “a tempo”, in A♭ major. There is no modulating bridge: the section empties and restarts.
transitions.evidence: The level falls from −15.8 dB at 3:30 to −33.7 dB at 4:00; the report has boundaries at 3:42 (0.54), 4:04 (0.71) and 4:42 (0.77), with the bass on C and 0.0–0.8 onsets per second at 4:05–4:35. The score marks letter L “Ruhig” with a timpani C and letter M “a tempo” (printed p. 79).

transitions.title: A swell from silence to a heavy tutti
transitions.how: After the quiet, exposed music at letters N and O, which carries the instruction “streng im Zeitmaß”, the level dips to −41 dB at about 6:00 and then swells. Within twenty seconds the whole orchestra is back near fortissimo, with winds and brass marked “marc. sempre” at letter P. The loud block runs for about a minute, through “Breit und wuchtig” and “immer breiter”.
transitions.evidence: The level is −41.1 dB at 6:00, −27.5 dB at 6:05, −13.8 dB at 6:20 and −9.9 dB at 6:30. The score marks letters P, Q and R “marc. sempre”, “Breit und wuchtig” and “immer breiter” (printed pp. 81–84).

transitions.title: Cut off, then the chorale returns
transitions.how: The tutti ends not with a cadence but with a drop: from −7.8 dB at 7:05 to −42.9 dB at 7:10, about 35 dB in five seconds. At letter S the score restores “Tempo I” and the quiet chorale returns, more than six minutes after its first appearance. In this reversed recapitulation the groups come back in the opposite order from the exposition, so the heavy tutti is heard before the chorale.
transitions.evidence: The level falls from −7.8 dB at 7:05 to −42.9 dB at 7:10, and the report has a boundary at 7:08 (0.65); a transposition-invariant chroma match between the opening chorale and 7:12 scores 0.65, against 0.45 or less at other windows. The score marks letter S “Tempo I” (printed p. 85); the reversed order is from the Hungarian Philharmonic note.

transitions.title: Another weighty tutti, marked “Breit”
transitions.how: After the returning chorale and an intermediate passage at letters T and U, the level stays between −22 and −33 dB until 8:20. At letter V the score marks “Breit” and the whole orchestra leaps to fortissimo, with winds and brass marked “marc.” Within twenty seconds the level climbs about 17 dB. The block lasts until about 9:05.
transitions.evidence: The report has a boundary at 8:20 (0.47); the level rises from −26.6 dB at 8:20 to −14.7 dB at 8:25 and −9.2 dB at 8:40. The score marks letter V “Breit” (printed p. 88).

transitions.title: The block stops; a quiet figure gathers
transitions.how: The broad tutti ends with a ritardando and diminuendo and a drop of about 12 dB in five seconds and about 21 dB in ten, from −10.4 dB at 9:05 to −31.7 dB at 9:15. At letter X, “a tempo”, the sound is pianissimo, and a quiet figure begins. Bruckner gathers the coda in stages: pianissimo at X, a long crescendo marked at letter Y, then a near silence at about 9:45 before the last broad peak.
transitions.evidence: The level is −10.4 dB at 9:05, −22.3 dB at 9:10 and −31.7 dB at 9:15, with a dip to −39.6 dB at 9:45. The score marks a “ritard.” before letter X “a tempo” and letter Y “poco a poco cresc.” (printed pp. 92–94).

transitions.title: A hush, and the timpani return
transitions.how: The last broad peak, marked “Sehr breit” just before letter Z, stops dead at about 10:27: the level falls from −11.6 dB to −31.4 dB in five seconds. The score then restarts at “Tempo I”, with the instruction “anfangs noch sehr ruhig” — at first still very calm. The timpani return after a long silence with an extended tremolo, and a crescendo builds over them to the final E major chord.
transitions.evidence: The level falls from −11.6 dB at 10:25 to −31.4 dB at 10:30; the report has boundaries at 10:26 (0.64) and 10:30 (0.59); the level then rises from −18.8 dB at 10:40 to −4.9 dB at 11:00. The score marks “Sehr breit” and, at letter Z, “Tempo I (anfangs noch sehr ruhig)” (printed p. 96); the timpani tremolo is from the Hungarian Philharmonic note.

source.title: Bruckner, Symphony No. 7, full score (Vienna: A. J. Gutmann, 1885, plate A.J.G. 576; first edition). The edition performed in the recording is not documented.
source.locator: IV. Finale, printed pp. 71–99. The Wagner tubas, played by horn players, are shown under “horns” because the section vocabulary has no separate entry. Entries are proportioned between the report’s anchors and approximate; passages not read from the score are left out.

timeline.note: Strings alone, pianissimo, on a tremolo and the first dotted figures.
Woodwinds join the strings as the first theme enters in its double-dotted rhythm.
The chorale in A♭ major: the strings carry the melody; Wagner tubas and horns later colour it.
The octave theme in A minor for the whole orchestra, heavily accented.
The ruhig hush: quiet wind figures pass from flute to oboe to clarinet, then Wagner tubas, over a timpani C; the strings rest.
The heavy tutti returns, winds and brass marked “marc. sempre”.
The quiet chorale returns at “Tempo I”, with winds and strings.
The broad tutti at letter V, “Breit”, for the whole orchestra.
The coda begins “anfangs noch sehr ruhig” over a timpani tremolo.
A crescendo for the whole orchestra over the timpani tremolo, to the final E major chord.

composer.epithet: A church organist who built symphonic movements from long harmonic spans, separate instrumental blocks and the silences between them.
facts: St Florian; harmony and counterpoint with Simon Sechter, 1855–61; form and orchestration with Otto Kitzler, 1861–63
Organist at St Florian and Linz Cathedral; Vienna Conservatory teacher from 1868; University of Vienna lecturer from 1875
Nine numbered symphonies, two earlier symphonies outside that sequence, masses, motets and other choral works
Several symphonies survive in distinct authorial versions, which later editors have treated differently
composer.background:
Bruckner was born in Ansfelden, near Linz, where his father was a schoolmaster and church musician. Teaching, organ playing and the parish liturgy belonged to the same local profession. After his father’s death in 1837, he became a choirboy at the Augustinian abbey of St Florian. The abbey gave him daily contact with sacred music and a large organ, but his first adult qualification was as a schoolteacher. He worked in small Upper Austrian communities before returning to St Florian in 1845. The later symphonist emerged from this practical church-and-school environment.

He became the abbey’s organist and moved to Linz Cathedral in 1855. By then he was thirty-one, yet he submitted himself to six further years of harmony and counterpoint study with Simon Sechter in Vienna, much of it conducted through written exercises and correspondence. Sechter’s discipline discouraged free composition while the technical work continued. Bruckner sought formal certification even after he had become an accomplished organ improviser. This extended apprenticeship matters when hearing a symphonic climax: its apparent mass rests on carefully managed lines, prepared dissonances and a bass that controls the rate of harmonic change.
